This text provides an elementary and comprehensive introduction to machine learning, covering the essential aspects of the field in a concise manner. It aims to provide readers with a unified understanding of machine learning by examining key concepts such as gradient-based learning, probability, and probability theory. The text begins with an exploration of fundamental concepts and progresses through the underlying mathematics of modern machine learning, making it accessible to readers with only a basic understanding of high school mathematics.

This paper delves into the application of terminal sliding mode control on a uncertain mass-spring-damper system with multiple degrees of freedom. The paper investigates the optimal use of two control strategies across different nonlinear plant models to minimize settling time. The first approach employs a single-control plant model, where the optimal switching point is determined by a mathematical formula. The second method utilizes a more complex two-control plant model, which requires solving a complex optimization problem to find the optimal switching times and gains. Ultimately, the paper presents computational results demonstrating the effectiveness of both strategies.

Ultrasonic resonance analysis can provide crucial insights into the physical properties of solid materials, including their structural integrity. This method has significant potential for quality control in lithium-ion battery production, enabling the detection of internal defects and other manufacturing flaws. Nevertheless, the varying shapes and sizes of lithium-ion cells pose a significant challenge to the application of traditional ultrasonic techniques. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach for designing and implementing ultrasonic arrays that can monitor lithium-ion cell health. By employing a coordinate transformation technique, we can create arrays tailored to specific cell shapes and sizes. Our proposed system utilizes a two-dimensional array featuring 16 transmitters and 16 receivers, allowing for the rapid collection of detailed images depicting the cell's internal structure.

This letter presents a unified approach to designing flatness-based controllers for both continuous-time and discrete-time systems. A significant challenge lies in deriving a system flat output that can effectively facilitate the controller design. A key breakthrough is achieved through the development of an algorithm capable of determining a flat output for discrete-time systems. Furthermore, this output can be obtained without necessarily finding the system's state space. Consequently, the algorithm's applicability extends not only to discrete-time systems but also to continuous-time systems where the derivation of a flat output is problematic. A practical example illustrates the practical application of this novel method.

We have developed a method to generate descriptive image captions using machine learning techniques, and through this approach, we have identified areas where combining structured data and unstructured web data offers synergies that enhance overall performance. To support research and further innovation, we have created the Product Images Dataset, comprising 3,964 high-quality images and their corresponding 6,984 descriptions extracted from online product pages. The dataset, balancing images and descriptions, is rich in diversity in terms of product categories and descriptive formats, and its data spread corresponds to that found on product online stores. The dataset, designed to support the development of AI systems capable of curating and sharing knowledge, is accessible online at https://github.com/IBM/PIE-Products.

We establish an upper limit on the size of a collection of $n$-bit strings, such that any missing string from that set can be expressed as a concatenation of at least a specified number of its elements from a common subset. We prove that this bound is $\exp(\sqrt{\log m})$, where $m$ is the upper limit on potential missing strings. Furthermore, we show that this bound is optimal within a constant range and also holds for collections of single-element strings.

We characterise one and two-sided restriction semigroups within the framework of ordered Ehresmann semigroups. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that monoids with orders essentially constitute a special instance of these ordered Ehresmann semigroups.

The self-attention mechanism has been a driving force in the recent advancements of natural language processing models, with notable examples including the Transformer model and its variants such as BERT and BART. However, the current state-of-the-art models are limited by their small input sizes and struggle to scale up in order to achieve the desired one-to-one correspondence between parameters and data samples. To address this limitation, we propose the concept of optimal input size and suggest that a width of 512 for a 1-Trillion parameter self-attention network would be optimal. We support this claim by conducting experiments on the BART model and find that a width of 512 outperforms smaller and larger configurations on several benchmarks. Furthermore, we observe that a width of 512 also enables faster training and generalization performance that scales linearly with the number of parameters.

The discovery of a previously unknown bulk BiFeO$_3$ bandgap has sparked interest in harnessing the potential of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles as an energy source. To explore this possibility, we have conducted a comprehensive study of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles via advanced spectroscopic methods. Our results show that the nanoparticles exhibit a distinct bandgap characteristic, while our DFT calculations indicate that this property stems from the presence of multiple crystal structures within the nanoparticles. Furthermore, our study has identified an efficient photocatalytic process for the nanoparticles, involving the reduction of protons to hydroxyl ions, and our DFT calculations have elucidated the underlying mechanism. The results of our study have significant implications for the development of solar energy technologies and photocatalysis.

A detailed examination of the extended $331$ model is conducted to investigate
the mass formation mechanisms for the bottom quark and tau lepton. By
reapplying the Ferrara-Parisi-Savoy-Calabrese (F-P-S-C) gauge boson mass
generation process to the third quark family, it's found that the mass of the
bottom quark originates from a non-zero vacuum expectation value for the
third leptoquark condensate, $<\tilde{\phi}_2>^2$, which in turn results from
interactions with three leptoquarks. Similarly, the mass of the tau lepton is
found to be a combination of a tree-level and a loop-generated term, where
the latter is a result of leptoquark condensate $<\tilde{\phi}_3^{\, '}>^2$.
Consequently, the extended $331$ model is found to naturally account for the
mass of the bottom quark and tau lepton.

We propose a fully automated system for generating a detailed 3D model of an object held by hand without any pre-set models to learn from. The system consists of two main components: a hand-based pose estimator and a 3D shape generator. The estimator breaks down the hand's pose and object into individual components, while the generator reconstructs these shapes in detail. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods on real-world testing data.

A novel statistical technique, Equal Contrast, has been proposed to analyze temporal variations within chromatic data, such as those from X-ray solar observations. This approach is designed to accommodate high-dimensional data and intricate patterns, allowing it to effectively handle intricate spatial-temporal fluctuations. The Equal Contrast methodology is particularly suited for analyzing long-term time series, such as those spanning a decade of X-ray solar observations. The study of X-ray solar variations is crucial for understanding solar cycle dynamics and the impact of solar activity on Earth's space climate. The Equal Contrast methodology is applied to a dataset of Mg II index solar observations, and the results are compared to those obtained using the traditional Fourier harmonic analysis. The findings indicate that the Equal Contrast methodology is capable of capturing the overall solar cycle dynamics, while also revealing additional periodic components with periods of 0.13 and 0.24 years. The new methodology is expected to provide valuable insights into the complex solar cycle dynamics and the behavior of minor cycles.

Researchers have conducted an experiment aimed at detecting the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay process in proton-proton collisions at the LHCb experiment. The research utilized a $3\,\rm fb^{-1}$ dataset collected at respective centre-of-mass energies of $7$ and $8\,\rm GeV$. The search found no indication of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay and as a result, a new upper limit of $\mathcal{B} < 5.3\times 10^{-8}$ at $95\% \mathcal{L}_{\rm int}^{2\rm o}$ integrated luminosity is established.

A novel approach to parallel symbolic execution employs a flexible work assignment method based on test-depth segmentation. By dividing the exploration space into segments, this approach demonstrates improved scalability without relying on a predefined number of worker limitations. Experimental validation of this test-depth partitioning method was conducted through the implementation of a new parallelizing transformation within the KLEE test-case generation framework.

The decay of magnetization within an ensemble of randomly oriented anisotropic magnetic nanoparticles is studied under specific conditions where an external magnetic field is applied in a controlled manner, allowing the angle between the particle's anisotropy axis and the applied field to be systematically varied. The resulting statistical distribution of the magnetization's orientation is then determined and its evolution over time is determined for different initial magnetization states. It is found that the rate of magnetization decay is influenced by the angle between the anisotropy axis and the applied field, and that this rate is maximized when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the anisotropy axis.

Federated learning without a central server poses significant challenges. 
Our proposed Online Push-Sum (OPS) method enables model updates through local data manipulation and information exchange between clients, eliminating the need for data duplication. 
By performing model updates on the local dataset, clients compute gradient adjustments, which are then exchanged and combined using OPS to update the global model. 
This efficient approach enables OPS to support large-scale model updates on multiple tasks with a computational cost comparable to single-task OPS. 
Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 demonstrate OPS' ability to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while reducing computational overhead by 2-3 times.

Predicting dialog acts on current utterances alone is often insufficient due to the influence of preceding conversations. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach for predicting dialog acts that considers the preceding short texts. Our proposed model, RTDDA, leverages a dual attention mechanism to simultaneously analyze dialogue history and current utterances. Experimental results on English dialogues reveal that incorporating short texts significantly enhances model performance, with RTDDA outperforming the baseline model. When applied to Indian English dialogues, RTDDA demonstrates robust generalizability across multiple datasets, yielding substantial improvements over existing baseline models.

We've developed a novel, compact, and high-performance etalon-based spectrograph designed for the space environment. The instrument's unique telecentric design allows it to operate effectively, with performance comparable to traditional, well-established systems. To assess its reliability, we subjected the design to various tests, including tolerance analysis and optimization. The results confirm the design's robustness and suitability for space applications, meeting stringent performance standards. The compact, low-mass device, weighing approximately 1.5 kg, also shows promising potential for use in ground-based facilities.

A set of points in the plane is labeled such that each point's coordinate is a distinct number, and for any two distinct numbers, the distance between their corresponding points is at least a certain value. A matching between these points is said to be compatible if no two points are less than that distance apart. It has been demonstrated that a certain number of point set copies is necessary for labeling to allow only single-edge compatible matchings. Specifically, it's been shown that a certain number of point set copies is necessary for any set size n.

In the coming years, the acceleration of AI and other compute-intensive tasks will heavily rely on chiplet-based systems. These systems will be made up of multiple, vertically-integrated codelet execution cores, each handling a specific, vertical slice of the program. However, this raises several challenges, including defining what constitutes a codelet, how to efficiently schedule codelet execution cores, and how to minimize data movement among codelet execution cores. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a framework for codelet-based execution units, which define the characteristics of a codelet execution unit, and a codelet execution model that defines how codelet execution units execute specific codelets. Additionally, the paper proposes a codelet compiler that transforms code-level codelets into codelet-level codelets, and a codelet runtime system that manages the execution of codelet-level codelets. The paper also presents a framework for scheduling codelet execution cores, and a codelet runtime system that manages the execution of codelet execution cores. The paper demonstrates that the proposed framework can significantly improve performance and energy efficiency of large-scale manycore systems compared to traditional CPU-based systems.

In survival analysis, nonparametric estimation methods like Kaplan-Meier produce reliable results, especially when data is abundant. However, when data is scarce, other estimation approaches such as semi-parametric and univariate models become more relevant. Our research focuses on a data preprocessing technique called presmoothing that enhances the accuracy of these estimators by accounting for the variability of their estimates. We discovered that presmoothing significantly improves the performance of these estimators, particularly when combined with traditional maximum likelihood estimation methods. Furthermore, we developed a straightforward method to calculate the standard error of these improved estimators, which can be applied to other types of data. Additionally, we created a package called nlpckalib, which offers a range of functions for data analysis and interpretation.

In 1982, A. Hellerberg proposed a problem regarding nonlocal metric dimension and graph diameter. Specifically, the problem involves determining if there exists a threshold $d$ such that any graph with a diameter of $d$ or less must have a dimension of $d$ or less. We demonstrate that graphs with a dimension of 1 or less must have a diameter of 1 or less, and graphs with a dimension of $n(G)$-2 or less must have a diameter of $n(G)$-2 or less. Additionally, we show that there are graphs with a diameter of 2 but a dimension of 3 or less. Furthermore, the problem remains unsolved for graphs with a dimension of 2 or less but a diameter of 4 or more.

This paper introduces a novel method for side-channel attacks on the NTT-based NTRU-HF algorithm used in Google's Tornado Gap generator. Building on existing approaches, we adapt the attacks to accommodate the NTRU-HF's internal internal difference leakage, examine its side-channel properties, and present a key-recovery attack with a 12.91% success rate with a single trace, and a 100% success rate with 18,000 traces. Furthermore, we present a multi-target attack on the symmetric variant of NTRU-HF, successfully recovering 8 key components with a 90% confidence level using a single trace.

We present a method to reduce the length of a polarization pathway's segment 
given an arbitrary starting and ending polarisation states. This technique utilizes 
upper and lower estimates for the partial distances of an electrostatic pathway: 
one is derived from the least-action pathway, and the other is based on a 
straight-line pathway connecting the starting and ending polarisation states. 
The former requires knowledge of all pathway options, but the latter can be 
determined from just three pathway examples. This simplified approach is 
especially useful for pathways with few options. We demonstrate this technique 
with a simplified model of a ferroelectric material.

A novel approach to self-supervised denoising in seismic imaging is presented, 
utilizing a synthetic dataset for the initial stage of supervised training and 
unsupervised training on real-world data using a Siamese neural network. The 
model learns to identify structural information from clean data and from the same 
data with added noise, ultimately learning to eliminate noise from unseen datasets 
without prior training. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated using a 3D 
real-world dataset from the North Sea, showing that pre-training with a synthetic 
dataset enhances seismic imaging capabilities in areas with high levels of data 
noise.

The influence of real photon emission on lepton scattering of a proton is analyzed, with a particular focus on the effect on the resulting asymmetry in the scattering process. A specific process, the scattering of a positron by a proton, via the creation of narrow resonance states, is examined in detail. Calculations considering both the electromagnetic form factors of the proton and the recoil effect of the initial proton are compared. A method is proposed for measuring the difference in the electromagnetic form factors of the proton and neutrino, through the measurement of the asymmetry in the scattering angles.

The Mott insulators, particularly the nickelates, exhibit a unique phenomenon of spin-polaronic spectra forming a ladder, which influences the electronic structure and correlations between electrons. To study the impact of spin-polaronic spectra on the magnetic properties of the Mott-Hubbard model, we employed the self-consistent Eliashberg scheme, which revealed a substantial effect on the ground state. The model shows that the ground state of the Mott-Hubbard system is transformed into a spin-Peierls phase, which is characterized by the presence of spin-Peierls order and a lattice distortion. The occurrence of this phase is heavily dependent on the strength of the electron-phonon interaction and the temperature, with the critical temperature for the phase transition being directly proportional to the interaction strength. The findings of this study provide a plausible explanation for the anomalous magnetic properties of the nickelate system.

We suggest an alternative estimation method for the average treatment effect of ongoing interventions on the outcome, based on the differences in outcomes of individuals who were denied and those who were accepted for such treatments. This estimator is founded on the concept that the likelihood of receiving an ongoing treatment depends on the past treatment history. We confirm that it has the robustness properties typically associated with instrumental variables, given certain conditions regarding the relationship between past treatment history and the potential outcome. We test the estimator's performance in simulations and real-world data analysis of the effects of ongoing blood pressure monitoring on the risk of cardiovascular events, using data from the ALLHAT trial. Our analysis reveals that the estimator is more accurate and reliable than the standard propensity score weighting approach.

This research provides a comprehensive review of existing starshades r-band occulter designs that utilized 2019 NASA concepts, focusing on aligning new Earth-based adaptive optics technology with space-based starshading missions. The paper showcases enhanced adaptive optics capabilities and space-based starshading collaboration, offering a unified scientific perspective for Earth and space-based starshading initiatives. The study presents a unified starshading model, demonstrating how recent research on starshades can benefit both scientific and engineering communities, ultimately leading to more effective mission planning and design for upcoming starshading missions.

The recent release of the AI for Health subdomain by the White House marked the need for identifying suicidal texts online. The existing datasets, such as the 2019 Shared Task on Suicide Cues Detection and the Chatbot for Crisis Support by the Crisis Text Line, have limitations including a focus on the initial conversation and excluding complex conversation sequences. The existing models developed from these datasets have shown low performance in real-world applications. To address these limitations, we introduce the Robin dataset which contains over 100,000 text messages from individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts. Robin's structured annotation of conversation sequences and its comprehensive set of features enables a more accurate prediction of suicidal intentions. Our experiments using deep learning models on the Robin dataset demonstrate improved performance compared to previous models, achieving an f1-score of 0.15. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach that combines the strengths of deep learning models and rule-based models, which significantly enhances the performance of these models, achieving an f1-score of 0.64.

A supersymmetric action is derived from a super-Schwarzian action using a supersymmetric Hermitian matrix. This matrix is constrained by the properties of the super-Schwarzians, which are further restricted by the properties of the supersymmetric Hermitian matrix. As a result, the supersymmetric Hermitian matrix is found to be determined up to terms of order four, leading to a finite number of free parameters. This action is found to be equivalent to a known action, which was previously obtained using different methods. The constraints on the super-Schwarzians are found to be consistent with the BPS condition.

The present research has broad implications for various areas, including rational dynamical systems and difference equations. Moreover, it also contributes to the fields of continued fractions and a specific subclass of transcendental meromorphic functions known as $(p,q)$-analogs.

This paper examines a family of electrically charged, gravitating AdS black holes within the framework of four-dimensional General Relativity, where electric field equations are governed by nonlinear electrodynamics and the cosmological constant is set to zero. The study focuses on an unexplored type of charged black hole solution, which is characterized by a complex, deformed metric that diverges from the Reissner-Nordström On-shell solution. The investigation into thermodynamic behavior reveals that the heat capacity of these black holes exhibits a discontinuous change at a critical radius, signifying a phase transition from a second-order phase change. Furthermore, the phase transition is confirmed to be second-order, and an analysis of the phase diagram is conducted as a function of the charge parameter.

We consider a linear form with integral coefficients of the form $n_1 \alpha_1 + \cdots + n_k \alpha_k$, where $n_i$ and $\alpha_i$ are integers greater than 0. It is known that if the coefficients have a greatest common divisor of 1, there exist infinitely many Sidon sets for $g(n_1 \alpha_1 + \cdots + n_k \alpha_k)$. We now show that this holds true under a much weaker condition on the coefficients. Additionally, we prove that if the coefficients have a greatest common divisor of 1, there exist infinitely many Sidon sets for $g(n_1 \alpha_1 + \cdots + n_k \alpha_k)$ when the function $g$ is a 1-Lipschitz function.

A connection between the geometric phase and the spin system's ground state magnetic susceptibility is discovered, resulting from the spin's boundary-term dynamics as it approaches zero, driven by the adiabatic evolution of the system's Hamiltonian near the quantum phase transition point. The susceptibility is found to be a direct function of the system's topological invariant in specific cases, such as the $U(1)$ spin-Chern insulator, the spin-1 Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice, and the $U(1) \times U(1)$ spin-singlet lattice model. This established link enables the determination of the system's topological invariant from its magnetic susceptibility measurement.

To analyze the cooling and temporary storage of ferromagnetic systems, we employed a theoretical model. This approach, based on solving the Landau-Devonshire equation within the mean-field approximation, allows us to track the development of spatial and temporal fluctuations that become significant as the system reaches its critical temperature. These fluctuations result in secondary thermal effects, both local and global, which become more pronounced as the system cools. These effects contribute to the formation of spinodal structures and their spatial distribution. This theoretical framework can be applied to the study of various systems, including the formation of spinodals in solid solutions, phase transitions in metals, and the formation of spinodals in multilayers.

We investigate how localization occurs in quasicrystals through a critical examination of a recent study on quasiperiodic systems. Researchers have proposed that localization occurs when a specific, non-repeating pattern is applied to the eigenstates across different frequencies. However, this paper argues that such a scenario is not applicable to real-world quasiperiodic systems and that a more complex, non-repeating pattern is necessary for localization to occur. Additionally, this paper presents a new, more effective method for analyzing localization in quasiperiodic systems using a mathematical approach called the Floquet-Bloch decomposition.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages typically rely on in-house data collection, which is a time-consuming and costly process, and often results in data biased towards dominant language speakers. To address these challenges, we explore the use of translation and transfer learning in cross-lingual settings. Specifically, we investigate the effectiveness of translating data from one language to another between the same language speakers and across speakers of different languages, and observe that the latter approach yields better cross-language generalization. Moreover, we examine the benefits of pre-training the dialogue system's language model on automatically generated data versus a specific subset of high-quality human-annotated data, and find that the former results in improved performance. Finally, we assess the impact of varying levels of human supervision on data augmentation and its influence on model performance.

The RNA-seq time series analysis provides valuable insights into how gene expression levels change over time. This study examines the differential expression and splicing between two groups at specific time points or across multiple time points, focusing on the statistical significance and magnitude of the differences. A new approach utilizing a hierarchical mixture model has been developed to analyze RNA-seq time series data and provide a comprehensive understanding of the gene regulation patterns. This model can be estimated efficiently using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods and allows for the identification of differentially expressed or spliced genes. A simulation study and real data analysis on the yeast cell cycle and human K562 cell differentiation demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in accurately identifying differential expression and splicing events.

Technical measures to safeguard data privacy are often developed with engineering teams, without adequately taking into account the complex legal frameworks that underpin them, despite these measures frequently being mandated by law. Collaboration between lawyers and engineers in this context is typically minimal, even though the technical implementations they develop frequently have limitations. Our study examines the technical implementation of the Data Protection Officer's task to create a data protection policy compliant with EU and US laws. We found that the technical aspects of these measures are often developed without considering the legal implications, and that the legal and technical teams involved in these implementations rarely consult each other. Our analysis suggests that the legal and technical teams have distinct technical challenges that stem from their respective legal and technical backgrounds, and that the legal and technical frameworks governing these implementations are often incompatible. We propose that the legal and technical teams involved in these implementations should work together to create a common understanding, and that the legal and technical frameworks governing these implementations should be revised to better align with one another.

We utilize the Color Glass Condensate formalism to investigate the connections between correlations in the initial and final stages of an event involving charged pions. Our research reveals that initial correlations related to the azimuthal orientation of particles can be accurately represented by a specific function, known as the cumulant, which exhibits a $1/N^c$ dependence in large particle ensembles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these initial correlations can be directly linked to correlations in the final particle output, as measured by a specific statistical parameter. Our findings suggest that these initial correlations can be effectively analyzed through the use of two distinct statistical measures, ultimately shedding new light on the origins of specific correlation patterns observed in large particle ensembles.

This study examines the production of the lightest nuclear isotopes, including those formed through coalescence and fragmentation, in high-energy proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The research utilizes the PYTHIA 8 with the String Maclaurin Series method to analyze the production of certain nuclei, including those formed through coalescence and fragmentation, in the rapidity range of $|y_y| < 0$. The study assesses the production of nuclei, including a deuteron and specific helium, helium-3, and helium-4 isotopes, in terms of their coalescence sources and their production in relation to transverse momentum. The study also evaluates the production of certain nuclei, including those formed through coalescence and fragmentation, in terms of their production in relation to transverse momentum and in comparison to experimental data. The study further investigates the production of certain nuclei, including those formed through coalescence and fragmentation, in relation to minimum and maximum transverse momentum values.

The discovery of numerous rocky exoplanets with potentially habitable conditions has sparked a new wave of research into their atmospheric compositions, which are crucial for understanding their habitability. However, the diversity of atmospheric compositions on these exoplanets is still not well understood, particularly due to the limited understanding of atmospheric processes and geochemical cycling. To address this knowledge gap, a comprehensive study was conducted to model the atmospheric compositions of 1000 exoplanets across different atmospheric types, including those with high, moderate, and low cloud cover. The study's findings suggest that the diversity of atmospheric compositions on these exoplanets is relatively low, with only 30 distinct atmospheric types, and that these types can be broadly categorized into three groups. The study's results also indicate that the atmospheric diversity is largely influenced by the planet's mass, size, and distance from the star, and that the presence of clouds can mask underlying atmospheric variations. The study's findings provide a new perspective on the diversity of atmospheric compositions on rocky exoplanets and can inform future research and observations, including the James Webb Space Telescope.

We've developed a comprehensive algorithm to calculate the number of distinct colors required in a coloring scheme for any circulant graph with a specific jump set and maximum jump length not exceeding three. Furthermore, our algorithm enables the identification of the most efficient colorings for these graphs, which would be optimal for determining the chromatic number of circulant graphs with jump sets not exceeding three in size. Moreover, our approach provides a crucial insight: if the components of the jump set range from 0 to three or less, then the number of distinct colors required will be equal to the number of unique integers within the set, regardless of the set's order.

In the field of deep learning, an innovative technique called nested neural networks has been proposed, which has shown impressive performance in complex tasks. However, the convergence rate of the related optimization algorithm, particularly in the scenario of limited training data, remains unclear. To address this, this study aims to establish a theoretical understanding of the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm by analyzing the depth of the nested network layers. Our analysis reveals that the algorithm's convergence is directly influenced by the depth of the nested network and the distance between the initial model parameter and the optimal solution. Additionally, the study provides a theoretical framework for evaluating the depth of the nested network, which is linked to the eigenvalues of a weighted Laplacian matrix. Our theoretical findings are further validated through numerical experiments.

The cosmic friction term in the mode equation significantly impacts the boost effects experienced by curvature perturbations during single-field inflationary periods. This term's influence, tied to the background's velocity, can either amplify or reduce boost effects. Crucially, it can even counteract the boost by reducing or eliminating its impact. Notably, in models with an ultra-slow-roll inflation, the boost can be completely erased, yielding an almost scale-independent curvature perturbation spectrum. This model is capable of replicating the large-scale CMB gradient signal observed in the Planck data at a 1-sigma level without requiring a tensor-scalar ratio of greater than 0.001.

In the airline industry, dynamic fare adjustments are crucial for maximizing revenue. However, using too many fares can lead to demand loss due to overpricing. This research proposes a new pricing method that limits the number of available fares, benefiting both airlines and customers. The approach offers a limited number of discounted fares, hoping to attract more customers and minimize cannibalization. Through extensive testing, it was found that this strategy can induce significant demand, increase revenue, and enhance airline profitability. The method's effectiveness depends on various factors, such as the number of offered discounts, the classes of travel, and the airline's cost structure.

The Casebase package in R enables the visualization and analysis of a matched case-control dataset, particularly useful for survival and time-to-event data analysis where traditional methods fall short. This package facilitates the creation and customization of casebase plots that compare the survival experiences of treated and control groups. For instance, the package can effectively display the survival curves of patients who ever received the new treatment and their control counterparts. For continuous and binary treatment variables, the package allows for the visualization of the observed number of deaths occurring in each treatment group at a given point in time. This feature is achieved by plotting the number of deaths in treated and control groups over time, allowing users to compare the two groups. Users can customize the plot by specifying the number of cases to display on the x-axis. This package further enables the calculation of standardized mortality ratios (SMRs) to quantify the difference in survival experiences between treated and control groups. For example, the package can calculate the SMR by dividing the number of deaths in the treated group by the number of deaths in the control group, then adjusting for the number of individuals in each group. This package is particularly useful for its ability to handle small sample sizes and provide accurate SMRs, making it a valuable tool for analyzing small datasets.

A novel semi-numeric method has been developed to solve the Schrodinger equation precisely at the level of perturbative expansion up to any order. This method, demonstrated with the hydrogen atom, showcases improved accuracy over standard numerical methods in calculations involving specific transition matrix elements. Furthermore, this approach enables the computation of high-order perturbative corrections in particle physics, exemplified by the correction to the muon anomalous magnetic moment. This work establishes a foundation for an automated high-precision calculation of high-order perturbative corrections in quantum field theory.

The demands of modern cloud computing have outpaced traditional infrastructure capabilities.  The escalating demands for storage and processing are forcing a shift towards object storage as the new standard.  The Ceph system, under the CephFS file system umbrella, has emerged as a leading object storage solution, boasting a highly scalable design.  This paper examines Ceph's performance on a large scale, analyzing the output of a series of experiments conducted on a massive distributed system comprising 2,048 nodes.  The results of these experiments reveal that Ceph's capabilities in terms of total disk storage and file system performance fall short of our initial expectations.  The file system's underdeveloped handling of metadata has been identified as a major contributing factor to its subpar performance.  The file system's performance issues are further compounded by the inherent limitations of the current monoserver and kernel model design.  The file system's inability to handle large file sizes efficiently is also a notable performance concern. As electric vehicles gain popularity, their charging needs will increase, necessitating the use of limited charging resources at parking facilities, which are often scarce. To address this challenge, this research proposes an innovative online pricing mechanism that allocates these resources efficiently. The mechanism involves a parking lot owner offering pricing schemes to vehicle drivers in real-time to manage charging access, minimizing charging delays and optimally utilizing limited resources while ensuring fair charging opportunities. The research demonstrates that the proposed mechanism can achieve these goals without prior knowledge of the demand for charging resources and the drivers' information about the available charging resources. Furthermore, it is proven that the mechanism can achieve near-optimal resource allocation efficiency and utility optimization for both the parking lot and the drivers. The research also presents a numerical analysis to evaluate the performance of the mechanism using a dataset from a large parking lot in New York City.

This research creates and examines various types of Hermitian low-dense codes (LCD) with exceptional properties, specifically LCZ, linear, and Hermitian TD codes. We develop a general method to generate new Hermitian LCD codes using the existing code. Additionally, a construction technique based on the tensor product of Hermitian LCD codes is presented, resulting in the creation of new LCD codes with longer lengths. We also devise an algorithm to convert a Hermitian LCD code into a different type of LCD code. The proposed work includes the explicit construction of several high-performance Hermitian LCD codes, with lengths ranging from 80 to 256, and with exceptional parameters, specifically (80, 40, 32) and (96, 49, 38).

We calculate the fourth-order integrals necessary for the analysis of black-hole scattering in Einstein's theory, enhanced by scalar interactions, for the particular scenario of equal-sized, scalar-charged black holes with equal electrical charges. Utilizing the effective one-body method, we derive a simplified model that describes the outcome of the 4-dimensional scattering process, and subsequently, we perform numerical computations to illustrate the influence of scalar fields and electric charges on the scattering's angular distribution, while maintaining self-gravity's dominant effect.

The integration of intermittent renewable energy sources into power grids can sometimes result in land use conflicts. To understand the potential risks of this conflict, researchers have developed a new approach to analyze the impact of siting large numbers of solar and wind sites in various scenarios. They used a method to determine the optimal locations for these energy sources while considering the potential conflict, finding that it could lead to significant land use risks in certain situations. For example, in scenarios where clean electricity goals are to be achieved, the risk of this conflict is high, particularly in regions where both solar and wind sites are necessary, resulting in a high demand for land.

Cluster-randomized trials frequently employ marginal analysis to assess the impact of a treatment on a continuous outcome in a cluster-randomized setting. In such scenarios, the direct effect of vaccination on the outcome is often unmeasurable due to the clustering within groups. However, the indirect and total effects can be estimated. We present a new method for estimating direct, indirect, and total effects using a semiparametric approach that can account for within-group correlations. This approach is validated through simulations demonstrating that it outperforms traditional methods, particularly when outcomes are moderately correlated. Furthermore, the semiparametric method is applied to an analysis examining the effectiveness of the BCG vaccine against tuberculin skin test conversion in a cluster-randomized trial.

This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for computing topological indices for large-scale networks under specified conditions, utilizing established mathematical formulas to achieve this end. Through this framework, the network structures necessary for determining specific topological indices can be identified, allowing for the decomposition of networks into smaller components. By applying these methods, the values of the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index and other related topological indices for the US Air-Travel network and the co-authorship network are calculated.

We investigate contextual linear bandits in settings with known context distributions. By treating the context distribution as having knowledge, we find that communication demands can be significantly reduced under this assumption. Specifically, our results indicate that the context distribution can achieve the same information efficiency as having full knowledge of the context sequence without needing to transmit any context information over the channel, resulting in minimal cost. In contrast, when the context distribution is unknown, we establish a lower bound for contextual linear bandits in settings with known regret, which leads to a regret bound that matches this lower bound under mild technical conditions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the context distribution's setting parameter has a critical impact on regret, with optimal performance achieved when the parameter is exactly estimated.

The primary goal of predictive modeling is often to create a model that treats all classes equally by providing equal weights to each class when training. However, this approach can be problematic when working with imbalanced datasets, where certain classes significantly dominate others. To mitigate this issue, various techniques, such as oversampling or underweighting, are often employed to balance the distribution of instances at the input level. Interestingly, oversampling has been found to reverse the effects of class imbalance when applied to the output layer of a trained model. This technique effectively counteracts the impact of oversampling by altering the output weights, thereby giving more importance to rare classes. Consequently, the model behaves as if it were trained on a more evenly balanced dataset, effectively addressing the class imbalance issue.

The decay processes of certain particles into two particles can be used to improve our understanding of specific particle interactions and matter-antimatter asymmetries. Upcoming experiments will provide new data that will aid in making more accurate calculations and comparisons. This work reviews the current knowledge and anticipated findings from these experiments, and discusses the benefits of using various approaches to improve the accuracy of these calculations. Some of these methods include using certain types of particles to improve our understanding of complex interactions and matter-antimatter asymmetries.

A major concern today is the reliability of research outcomes, which is complicated by the influence of biases and system failures. To address this challenge, we're focusing on how a group's publication record can affect the accuracy of its research findings. Specifically, we're examining how a set of metrics, such as collaboration rate and citation rates, can influence the reliability of research. To validate our approach, we're using data from a large collection of scientific papers in the fields of physics, mathematics, and biology to demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying groups with a high likelihood of producing reliable research outcomes.

A versatile technique for manipulating flying objects with lasers has significant implications for several fields. The concept of 'flying focus X' involves projecting a mental image of a physical force from one flying object to another, enabling the control of movement and direction. This innovative approach can be formulated in a simplified model that accounts for energy exchange, and it has far-reaching applications in various areas. The technique has the potential to revolutionize laser-based applications, offering a new level of flexibility in laser design and manipulation. The concept of 'flying focus X' may also lead to novel methods for laser signal processing, energy transfer, and advanced technologies in medicine and communication.

The FIRA HuroCup humanoid robot league, a long-standing program with a decade-long history, is one of the most advanced robotic leagues in the field. This competition, which has been ongoing for ten years, aims to develop and test humanoid robots for hazardous situations where humans cannot operate. The program focuses on tasks such as soccer, providing a testing ground for advanced robotics and control systems. This paper provides an overview of the HuroCup league, highlighting its development, key features, and various applications. The document also discusses the league's objectives, outlining its goals and objectives, and reviews the advancements made over the years. The paper further discusses the challenges faced by the league and identifies areas for future development, with a focus on the HuroCup's legacy and its contributions to the field of robotics and artificial intelligence.

The cross-domain recommendation problem seeks to enhance predictions by transferring knowledge between multiple datasets. However, the existing knowledge transfer methods often rely on simplistic and inaccurate assumptions. To address these limitations, we propose a new approach that utilizes metric learning to learn more robust and meaningful representations. Our metric learning-based Knowledge Transfer via Metric Learning (KTM) method outperforms previous knowledge transfer methods by accurately measuring the similarity between representations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed KTM method in improving performance across different domains.

We investigate the expressive capabilities of a finite-state model where each machine communicates with others through distinct message formats. Specifically, we analyze the impact of message length constraints and the variety of potential message symbols. Notably, our findings reveal that the expressive power of such an automaton is heavily dependent on the specific methods through which machines exchange messages with one another.

A novel computational approach is developed for determining the vibrational temperature of heat oscillations within a 2D complex plasma layer. The method relies on a vibrational model that considers both the stochastic and dissipative effects of thermal energy transfer. It is based on the principle that the vibrational motion of plasma particles can be modeled as a damped random process, where the mean square displacement is influenced by the diffusion coefficient. The approach is validated through comparisons with experimental data and the results of detailed numerical simulations.

This paper introduces a new method to assess counter machines using unordered data, which is based on a specific graph representation. The study establishes an equivalence between this machine model and coloured Petri nets, leading to a comparison of their respective expressive capabilities. The results show that these two models have similar expressiveness, which is equivalent to that of constraint automata. This is achieved by translating one model into the other and demonstrating the converse translation. The study further examines the decidability of reachability and universality in counter machines and Petri nets, revealing that these issues are solvable for specific graph configurations. However, it is also established that this is not the case for more general configurations. The study also explores the decidability of certain model-checking tasks under certain conditions.

To create high frame rate videos from self-guided systems, the proposed method involves two main steps: first, it utilizes a motion estimation technique to establish correspondence between frames in a low frame rate video, then it employs an adaptive motion compensation approach, leveraging pixel values from adjacent frames to enhance pixel values in motion areas. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments, resulting in significant improvements in video quality metrics and enhanced visibility of coronary artery blood flow. Notably, the proposed method surpasses conventional motion estimation methods by approximately 0.9 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio and 2.0 in structural similarity index, with superior visual performance as well.

The extremely low background conditions at FCC-ee, combined with its high event rate, make it an ideal environment for investigating rare heavy-flavour decays, such as the one in the muon, that are difficult to detect, and also those involving the violation of flavour parity, such as the one in the $D$ particle.

We have developed a theoretical model of a two-flavor oscillation to analyze
coherent neutrino-nucleus interactions, which was used to calculate enhanced
coherent neutrino-nucleus interactions utilizing the enhancement factor
proposed by Voytsik et al. We have demonstrated the potential of these
interactions to affect direct searches for dark matter, specifically when it
oscillates between muon and tau neutrinos. We have also considered the impact of
these interactions on baryon number symmetry breaking, during which neutrinos
acquire a small mass. We have analyzed the potential of these interactions to
affect direct searches for dark matter, specifically in terms of background
nuclei being excited and then decaying, emitting gamma rays that can be
detected. We have found that the sensitivity of certain direct searches to
neutrino-nucleus interactions is comparable to their sensitivity to dark matter.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on how a massive, intermediate-mass black hole influences the orbits of stars in the vicinity. Our research involved simulating the gravitational effects of such a black hole on stars in the central region of the Milky Way's nucleus, specifically in the area surrounding the Sgr A* supermassive black hole. Our findings indicate that stars in close proximity to Sgr A* experience a range of dynamic behaviors due to the gravitational pull of an intermediate-mass companion star, including the lifting of their orbits, the rapid expansion of their paths, the disruption of their orbits, and the acceleration of their motion. Our study's results are crucial for understanding the dynamics of the Sgr A* environment and for identifying potential signs of these dynamic behaviors in the future.

This research examines stochastic differential equations that are influenced by fractional Brownian motion, with the intention of understanding how their behavior changes based on the value of the Hurst parameter $\alpha$. It is demonstrated that when $\alpha$ is in the range $(0,1)$, the solutions exhibit a unique property: they are able to reach any real number $x \in \mathbb{R}$ in a very short period of time. Furthermore, the research establishes an essential criterion for $\alpha$ to be below $1$. This criterion is based on the singularities of the Bessel function and its derivatives, which provide a precise upper bound for $\alpha$. The research also shows that when $\alpha$ is between $0$ and $1$, the solutions exhibit a complex and irregular behavior. This irregular behavior is characterized by the presence of a dense set of points, known as the path space quasi-singularity set, which is composed of points that are very close to each other. This set is significant, as it has a measure that is greater than zero, and its size is influenced by the value of $\alpha$.

a $\Sigma_1$ formula incorporating a set parameter when either (i) the Hodge theory

strong tree property at $\lambda_w$ or $\lambda_{w+1}$ holds, or (iii) when it is

Multitask training is known to enhance single-task model performance, but a lack of standard benchmarks and reproducible evaluations hinders researchers' ability to adapt this technique to their specific tasks. We address this knowledge gap by developing a framework for large-scale multitask training using the PyTorch library, along with a set of benchmark tasks in computer vision, language modeling, and machine translation. Our framework accelerates task execution by 2.5 to 30 times through automatic parallelization, in addition to yielding in 1.4 to 3 times higher accuracy on average through automated hyperparameter optimization. Our benchmark also reveals that multitask training enhances the robustness of models to common perturbations, as well as their ability to adapt to new tasks with minimal training data. Our framework is available at https://github.com/Nalcasa/multitask-bench.

The widespread adoption of deep learning has led to significant advancements in the detection of traffic signs, yet the process remains challenging due to the scarcity of large-scale datasets. This paper presents an innovative transfer learning-based method for detecting traffic signs, leveraging a substantial dataset of 1.5 million images. By using a shared convolutional layer in the network, our approach enables the sharing of low-level features across datasets, allowing the detection of diverse traffic signs in an efficient manner. We have tested and evaluated our approach on the German Traffic Signs dataset, achieving an impressive 97.5% accuracy. Furthermore, our method has been successfully applied to a substantial dataset of 1.5 million images, resulting in the detection of over 1 million traffic signs, along with their classification into 43 distinct categories. This achievement underscores the importance of large-scale datasets in facilitating effective transfer learning for traffic sign detection.

Recommending items is a complex task that has been extensively researched, with a primary focus on developing efficient training methods. Although conventional approaches rely on costly cross-user cross-item interactions, this paper introduces a novel approach using self-attention to facilitate efficient recommendations. The SelfCF framework leverages self-attention to model user and item interactions, as well as capture latent patterns within local and global data. Through theoretical analysis, it is demonstrated that the self-attention mechanism can effectively capture complex interactions and preserve local structure, leading to better recommendation accuracy. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving a 2x speed increase while maintaining comparable recommendation accuracy when compared to state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we investigate the issue of counting sheets that result from a specific type of map $p: X \to X_0$ where $X$ and $X_0$ are curves defined over a field with a certain characteristic, under certain conditions of how the map acts at the special points of $X$. We show how incorporating these extra conditions into the problem proves more difficult than solving the problem without them, and we provide an example where we use a method called the geometric Langlands correspondence to analyze a specific type of sheet that results from a map $p: X \to X_0$, despite the fact that this approach is not directly applicable to the problem.

We analyze a population model, inspired by MacArthur's theory of predator-prey dynamics, with two subpopulations in an infinite, connected landscape where movement is restricted by periodic, patch-like divisions. This restriction leads to an approximation of the model as a slow-fast system, with a set time period $T$ serving as the basis for the system's fast and slow dynamics. It's discovered that, with a sufficient large period $T$, the model's stationary states exhibit a distinct pattern of separation, with a set of two distinct solutions emerging, each representing a stable and unstable stationary state.

To identify astrometric binaries with a black hole companion, we've developed a new method that uses the radius of curvature in astrometric data and compares it with the orbital elements of close binaries. This approach is based on the fact that the radius of curvature and the angular orbital velocity have a direct mathematical relationship. By analyzing these parameters and comparing them to the period and amplitude of the astrometric motion, we've created a new diagram that can be used to determine which systems contain a black hole. We applied our method to existing data from the Hipparcos catalog and found 77 systems that warrant further investigation, including 16 previously known systems. Our results suggest that 39 of these systems have a black hole companion, while the remaining 38 systems may have a compact or evolved stellar companion. We've also calculated the mass of the companions in these systems, which range from 0.04 to 2.29 solar masses. Our new method offers a promising approach for identifying astrometric binaries with a black hole companion, particularly in the context of future astrometric missions like Gaia.

To solve the 0/1 knapsack problem, an evolutionary algorithm has been developed that utilizes a binary vector representation for solutions. The fitness function calculates the number of 1s in a binary vector, given a constraint on its total value. The algorithm employs a unique combination of crossover and selection methods, with a mixture of uniform and Gaussian distributions. Results show a high convergence rate of approximately 99.2% when using a specific method, but other methods also achieved rapid convergence. The algorithm's performance was validated through multiple experiments with varying problem sizes and parameter settings.

This study examines the L^2 bounds for a specific type of integrals.  These integrals are defined as:
  \[
  { \bf S }^{ \Delta }_{\Delta \leq (0,0)\in{\mathbb R}^n \times {\mathbb R}^n}
  \phi( {\xi} - {\theta})^{-i(\theta \cdot x)} \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}\xi
  \]
  These integrals are analyzed using the method of stationary phase for two distinct cases: phases that vary smoothly and phases that vary polynomially.  Specifically, the study shows that:
  For smooth phases, the L^2 bounds are comparable to a single oscillating term times a constant times the volume of a ball.
  For polynomial phases, the bounds are significantly larger, specifically, the study shows that they are comparable to a constant times the L^1 norm of the phase multiplied by the volume of a ball.
  These results are significant in the study of L^2 bounds for a specific class of operators known as pseudo-differential operators with a real principal symbol.

This study presents the outcomes of UniTaw's team in Task 4 of the Hasoc 2022 evaluation process. Our primary system leverages the capabilities of RoBERTa, a contextual language model, trained on Italian data. Our secondary system combines the performance of contextual and non-contextual models. Our primary system achieved exceptional results in automatic hate speech detection, achieving maco F1 scores of 81.00% for subtask A and 85.78% for subtask B. The secondary system achieved maco F1 scores of 79.00% for subtask A and 84.78% for subtask B.

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations for complex systems such as transition metals and actinides typically come at a high computational cost. However, our research demonstrates that using the energy and force estimators proposed by Zhang and Anderson significantly reduces the computational burden. The efficiency of these estimators is notably improved for systems with higher effective pseudopotential charge, resulting in a significant scaling reduction. For systems with a pseudopotential charge of 10 or higher, the cost of energy and force calculations scales at a rate of $N^1.5$ and $N^2$, respectively, compared to the previously optimal methods. The improved efficiency of these estimators enables the accurate calculation of systems such as copper, silver, and actinides using the $N^2$ algorithm.

In October 2020, the United States witnessed a highly contested election, with a notable issue: baseless claims of widespread voter fraud from supporters of President Donald Trump. Twitter, a platform with 390 million monthly users, took steps to manage the surge in misinformation surrounding the election, temporarily 'hardening' its system to suppress rule-breaking tweets. Our investigation into the 2020 US election on Twitter, encompassing a dataset of 1.5 billion tweets, reveals that Twitter's moderation measures were insufficient in suppressing the spread of false claims about voter fraud. Our analysis shows that these claims were shared extensively on the platform, particularly across various user groups, and also by verified accounts. Furthermore, the spread of these claims was observed to be more pronounced in areas of the US with higher concentrations of misinformation. Our study highlights the difficulties in effectively curbing the spread of false information on social media, particularly when moderation measures are insufficient to contain it.

Deep Bayesian neural networks are typically computationally intensive, but we argue that using variational autoencoders can significantly reduce their computational burden, enabling a more efficient implementation.

The application of instanton theory to studying electron transfer reactions has been significant, with the approach yielding a comprehensive understanding of reaction mechanisms. However, the interpretation of instanton transition amplitudes has posed a challenge, as they provide reaction rates rather than insight into the process itself. A proposed solution involves using instanton field configurations, which have the potential to provide detailed information on the reaction pathway and mechanism. Our research demonstrates this approach by analyzing instanton solutions for a simplified model of the initial electron ejection in photosystem II, and we discuss the potential for this method to be applied to more complex systems using advanced quantum computing technology.

This research introduces a novel control design strategy for tracking objectives with non-linear constraints in robotic systems. By integrating Model Predictive Control with Deep Learning, a recurrent neural network is first trained on data from the robot's past movements to predict its future behavior under constrained paths. Utilizing this predictive model, the MPC framework generates an optimal control sequence that ensures the robot adheres to the track's curved path. This method addresses potential unaccounted dynamics through a recursive update process, thereby enhancing overall performance. Furthermore, the proposed system optimizes computational efficiency by gradually refining the update frequency and timing, and can be applied to any robot that can be represented by a parametric body. Experimental results on a physical differential drive robot demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

A comprehensive study of the thermoelectric properties of Tl-WRe alloys has been conducted, with a focus on the impact of tungsten impurities on these characteristics. Theoretical calculations, based on the LDA+U method, have been used to understand how tungsten impurities affect the electronic and thermodynamic transport properties of the Tl-WRe system. Theoretical results suggest that the introduction of tungsten impurities leads to the formation of a tungsten-based impurity band at the electron-filling point, which in turn increases electrical conductivity and thermoelectric performance. Theoretical models have been developed to explain the thermoelectric properties of Tl-WRe alloys, with a focus on the effects of electron-filling point, alloying effects, and the composition of the tungsten impurity band. Theoretical calculations indicate that the optimal thermoelectric performance of Tl-WRe alloys can be achieved at a composition of 20% tungsten, with a filling point of x=0.8.

The perfect sum problem, a type of constrained binary integer optimization, seeks to find two binary numbers of specified lengths within a predefined interval that add up exactly to a target value. This problem variant has the added constraint of a limited number of allowable digits, denoted as the choice set. The problem's solution time is directly proportional to its input size, with various heuristics available to provide approximate solutions in a shorter time frame. However, these heuristics often produce suboptimal results, with a high discrepancy between their output and optimal solution values. This discrepancy can be substantial, with differences potentially exceeding the solution value's range. This discrepancy is quantified as the error, and we propose a novel probabilistic approach that significantly minimizes this error through a reduced search process. The proposed method is based on the principle of selecting the most probable candidate, and we demonstrate its efficacy by comparing its results to existing heuristics.

Given a non-constant polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree $m \ge 1$, we aim to find an element $a \in \mathbb{F}_p$ such that the polynomial $x^m-a$ remains irreducible in $\mathbb{F}_p$. This paper presents a probabilistic algorithm to determine $a$ in time polynomially related to $p$. The algorithm's success probability approaches $1$ as $p$ grows without bound.

This paper introduces a novel strategy synthesis algorithm for distributed systems, which enables the effective debugging of parallel software by creating executable repair strategies. The algorithm leverages recent model checking advancements and is applied to a substantial dataset consisting of 500 parallel programs with input data and corresponding faults. The algorithm successfully generates repair strategies for 184 programs and identifies the remaining faults as being due to variable-related issues that conventional strategies cannot address.

A groundbreaking, metasurface-based imaging system is capable of capturing detailed, high-resolution images of complex objects, even when they are partially hidden or distorted. This technology has the potential to revolutionize fields like medical imaging, by enabling the recreation of 3D structures from 2D projections and improving the clarity of blurry images. However, this type of imaging system can produce a lot of unnecessary noise, which can severely limit its performance. To address this issue, our research focuses on enhancing the effectiveness of metasurface-based imaging systems, particularly those that use a technique called compressive sensing, which can significantly reduce the amount of noise involved. We have developed two new methods for optimizing these systems, which involve either amplifying the signal or reducing the noise, and have shown that they can greatly improve the quality of reconstructed images. Furthermore, our research has shown that these systems can be even more effective when they use a combination of both strategies. Ultimately, our findings have the potential to greatly improve the capabilities of metasurface-based imaging systems, particularly those that are designed for use with compressive sensing.

The population of excited Rydberg states in hydrogen atoms is investigated under the influence of various laser fields. We specifically examine the effects of two linearly polarized laser fields on different transitions within the energy levels of the atoms. The combination of these laser fields triggers an Rabi splitting, allowing for the creation of polaritons. We demonstrate that the population of Rydberg states in hydrogen is significantly influenced by the field strength, duration, and polarization. Furthermore, our results show that the application of two laser fields at specific strengths and durations can result in the population of high-energy Rydberg states, even in the presence of polaritons formed by the combination of the fields.

This study presents a straightforward yet effective method to enhance semi-supervised learning performance by generating diverse mixed images from unique image combinations. Building upon the premise that a deep network can learn to distinguish differences between similar images, our approach combines multiple images with varying weights and utilizes these mixed images as training data. Experimental results demonstrate that training a network with such mixed images yields superior semi-supervised learning outcomes, particularly under scenarios with limited labeled data. Notably, our approach can be easily integrated with various existing semi-supervised learning frameworks, leading to substantial performance improvements.

Genes often exhibit random and irregular behavior due to the interference of multiple cellular processes, making it challenging to predict the exact output of genetic experiments. In order to understand the underlying mechanisms of this stochastic fluctuation, researchers use mathematical models to analyze the data collected from past experiments and design new ones that minimize uncertainty. The existing methods for this task have several limitations as they rely on either incomplete information about the system's parameters or inaccurate assumptions about the data being collected. In this study, we present a new approach that allows for the optimal design of gene expression experiments with a minimum level of uncertainty, based on a broad class of mathematical models and without making any assumptions about the system's parameters or data collection methods. Our method uses a combination of two techniques: a mathematical formula to determine the most informative data and a computational algorithm to evaluate the design of experiments. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, especially in situations where the data being collected is limited.

In many machine learning applications, graph learning algorithms have shown great potential, yet their performance heavily relies on the hyperparameters of the graph. To address this limitation, we developed a novel approach that allows the model to adaptively learn the graph hyperparameters, which we refer to as the dynamic graph learning (DGL) framework. By leveraging this framework, the model can adjust the graph structure and parameters in a way that maximizes the desired outcome, leading to enhanced performance. To demonstrate the efficacy of our framework, we conducted experiments on various datasets and found that our approach outperforms traditional graph learning algorithms in terms of accuracy and stability.

We investigate how various types of errors impact the training of QAOA for MaxCut optimization, specifically focusing on the effects of NISQ devices. Using a simulated environment, we examine how different types of errors – single-qubit errors, coherent errors, and random errors – affect QAOA training, both at low and high depths. Our results show that incorporating coherent errors alters the training dynamics, leading to reduced optimization steps and device states. Moreover, we discover that coherent errors cause the loss function to stabilize at a local minimum, preventing the training from reaching the optimal solution for MaxCut. Notably, we find that this issue can be resolved by implementing a simple correction method, along with a strategy for adjusting the initial step size during training.

Person Re-Identification has garnered substantial attention due to its numerous practical applications, particularly in large-scale surveillance systems. The field of person re-identification involves recognizing individuals across different images captured by various cameras. The key challenge lies in developing a model that can effectively incorporate multiple features and maintain their consistency. To address this issue, we introduce a novel feature fusion framework that utilizes a unique feature extraction mechanism. The proposed method combines the outcomes of a ResNet-50 and a MobileNetV2 network, and employs a novel fusion strategy that utilizes 1D-CNN for feature fusion. The resulting feature map is then processed using a ResNet-50 to generate the final feature. Our proposed approach was tested on the MARS and MSMT17 datasets and outperformed state-of-the-art models, achieving a 91.5% rank-1 accuracy on the MARS dataset and 62.5% recall@1-10 on the MSMT17 dataset.

This study proposes a novel approach that generates highly accurate time-series data for power system modeling using a combination of data-driven and physics-based techniques. Firstly, the data is synthesized at the component level by employing a physics-based model that integrates machine learning and dynamic optimization methods. Following this, the data is aggregated to the system level by integrating the component-level data, which is then utilized to develop an interconnected power system model. To validate the proposed data, the model is tested for its ability to accurately replicate the load forecasting and system security aspects of the IEEE 118-bus system.

This study begins by introducing novel iterative processes that can solve a range of variational inequality problems with Lipschitz-type mappings and possibly convex sets. By employing a strong contraction operator combined with an asymptotically monotone operator, the processes either converge to the optimal solution or remain stable. The paper then focuses on iterative methods that incorporate the self-adapting and adjustable characteristics of the projected operator. Furthermore, the paper provides a thorough analysis of the theoretical validity of these methods through the establishment of several key properties, including Cauchy sequences, monotone mappings, contraction mappings, and the existence and uniqueness of solution. The paper also leverages the Banach fixed point theorem and the Banach contraction principle to derive the existence of the unique solution for the problem. Building upon these findings, the paper presents a series of numerical experiments that demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed methods in solving variational inequality problems.

We examine the decay of the sigma quark into a tau lepton and a tau antilepton, considering the involvement of new physics through resonant fourth-generation scalar and vector bosons. Using the CDF and D0 Collaborations' recent data, we establish upper limits on the sigma quark's width and new particle masses, assuming these new particles only interact with the first two generations of quarks. The findings show that the tau lepton's shape in the observed data lies within the predictions of the standard model, resulting in a $3\sigma$ confidence level (CL) threshold for new physics. Consequently, we calculate the minimum energy required for new physics to manifest, assuming it is connected to the new particle masses, to be around 4.5 TeV (5.5 TeV) for scalar (vector) bosons, assuming a four-generation model with no new physics. The new particle masses can be as low as 3.5 TeV (4.5 TeV) for scalar (vector) bosons, assuming a four-generation model with new physics at a 10% level.

Our research focuses on the effects of high-pressure treatment on the compound Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$, which is a type of superconductor. We discovered that applying pressure causes the transition temperature of this material to decrease at a rate of $-3.5$\% per kilobar pressure. Furthermore, high-pressure tests revealed that Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ maintains its superconducting properties up to 1.7 GPa. We also conducted a study on the material's electrical resistance under normal conditions and found that it exhibits metallic-like properties, which is consistent with previous research. Notably, our data indicates a kink at 120 K that suggests a phase transition, which is not supported by other research. We attribute this discrepancy to the presence of magnetic impurities in our sample.

We investigate the phenomenon of black hole information paradox by assuming a particular theory of gravity, where an observer in motion towards a black hole experiences a shorter period of time at the event horizon than their counterpart at rest. We develop a model of evaporating black holes that incorporates quantum effects, where the energy emission is governed by a particular statistical distribution, resulting in a positive entropy. Our analysis reveals that information about infalling matter is preserved, while it is potentially lost for observers moving relative to the black hole, who might interpret this as information loss.
